summary:
TerraMatch is a browser-based discovery tool for finding candidate Earth analogs of lunar and Martian terrain. Instead of relying only on familiar analog sites, Automatic Search samples Earth locations and compares their measured terrain with 6,000 indexed areas on each selected planetary body. Manual Search supports investigation of a chosen Earth location.

Using NASA MOLA and LOLA elevation products alongside openly distributed Earth terrain data, TerraMatch compares slope distributions and elevation range at a common regional scale. Users can inspect location pairs, understand their similarities and differences, trace the underlying sources, export evidence, and explore source-derived terrain in an interactive 3D expedition.

The project turns large planetary datasets into an accessible workflow for identifying and explaining potential terrestrial testing environments. Results are candidates for further geological, literature, and field assessment; similarity scores do not certify a new analog or mission suitability. This helps students and researchers move from a possible match to a transparent, testable research question.
details:
What we built

TerraMatch is an interactive web application for discovering and explaining candidate terrestrial analogs of lunar and Martian terrain. It addresses the challenge by helping users investigate locations beyond a small catalogue of well-known analog sites.

Our focus is regional terrain: how slopes are distributed and how much elevation varies within an area. A terrestrial analog does not need to reproduce every planetary condition to be useful. TerraMatch therefore asks a specific question: where on Earth can we find terrain characteristics resembling a selected lunar or Martian landscape, and what evidence supports that comparison?

How it works

Automatic Search lets users choose the Moon, Mars, or both, together with a terrain condition. The application samples Earth locations within the chosen search region, retrieves their elevation data, and compares eligible areas against 6,000 indexed coordinate areas on each selected planetary body.

The planetary search index is derived from NASA Mars Global Surveyor MOLA and Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter LOLA elevation products. It is not a manually assembled list of successful matches. Earth elevation is obtained from publicly distributed Mapzen/Tilezen terrain tiles, which combine data from several underlying providers.

After identifying promising pairs, TerraMatch loads their regional elevation grids and recalculates the comparison. Users can select a pair to inspect its coordinates, slope measurements, elevation range, similarities, differences, and source records.

Manual Search provides a complementary workflow: users can enter an Earth place name, coordinates, or select a point on the globe to investigate a location directly.

Making the comparison understandable

Automatic pair comparisons use nominal 32 × 32 km study areas, a common 2 km analysis grid, and a 4 km slope baseline. Finer reference comparisons retain their documented sampling; comparisons involving different grid spacings use the coarser common grid.

The default terrain index combines slope-distribution similarity and relative relief, using weights of 65% and 35%. Relative relief is the difference between the highest and lowest elevations within an area. We compare regional terrain characteristics rather than treating absolute elevations on different planetary reference surfaces as interchangeable.

The Compare tab explains the selected pair before presenting detailed analysis. Planet overview provides planetary imagery, dimensions, and available data context. Sources connects the comparison to its underlying datasets, processing records, and limitations.

Users can export comparison reports and evidence records for further investigation.

Interactive exploration

The Expedition view provides an interactive 3D environment for exploring the selected area's source-derived terrain. Users can navigate the landscape and inspect surface, slope, elevation, and available temperature views to better understand local terrain characteristics.

Regional terrain heights come from the identified elevation products. Visual elements support exploration and interpretation, with their sources and limitations documented separately. The experience supports terrain understanding and comparative investigation; it does not establish landing safety, vehicle performance, or mission suitability.

Benefits and intended impact

TerraMatch makes planetary terrain data accessible to students, educators, researchers, and teams developing analog-study ideas. It provides a repeatable path from a possible location match to an evidence-based research question.

Candidate locations could support further investigation of regional mapping exercises, observation planning, or field-operation workflows. Geological relevance, access, permissions, and field safety require separate assessment.

The project's contribution is the combination of coordinate-based discovery, explainable comparison, traceable evidence, and interactive exploration in one browser-based workflow.

Tools and implementation

TerraMatch uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript ES modules, Three.js, WebGL, and Node.js processing and verification scripts. The application is hosted through GitHub Pages at terramatch.earth.

Planetary elevation values are distributed in losslessly compressed tiles so the browser can load relevant areas without requiring a new backend. Source metadata, product labels, and integrity hashes support traceability. Browser storage retains supported Earth search results and field notes.

Scientific boundaries

Search coverage is sampled and bounded, rather than an exhaustive scan of all three worlds. A high terrain index identifies a candidate relationship; it is not a probability, proof of novelty, or approval for a mission or permanent base.

Source grids may contain interpolation, and output spacing does not establish measurement accuracy. Regional elevation data do not resolve individual rocks or rover-scale hazards. Temperature and environmental records are presented separately where available and do not enter the terrain index.

TerraMatch supports the discovery and characterization process. Claims that a candidate is a new or less-known analog still require literature review, relevant geological evidence, and potentially field investigation.
